definition: Existing only on the surface, or dealing only with what is obvious rather than what lies deeper.
example: The storm left only superficial damage: a few scratched shingles and a bent gutter.
nuance: Cursory stresses haste, while superficial stresses a lack of depth, whether in a wound, an analysis or a friendship.
prompt: A student writes a book report the night before it is due.
options: Her report offered a superficial plot summary and never touched the novel's themes.
Her report was so superficial that the teacher cut three unneeded, repetitive paragraphs.
Her superficial report traced each theme with real depth through every single chapter.
Her report was superficial only because she printed it on thick, glossy paper.
reasons: Recapping events while ignoring the book's ideas stays at the surface.
Unneeded extra material is superfluous, a look-alike word that means something different.
Exploring themes thoroughly is the opposite of staying on the surface.
The paper's finish has nothing to do with how deeply the book was explored.

practice.prompt: A school nurse checks a boy who fell off his bike on the playground.
options: The scrape counted as superficial only because it was on his left knee, not his right.
The scrape on his knee was superficial, so the nurse simply cleaned and bandaged it.
The cut was so superficial that he needed surgery to repair a torn tendon underneath.
The nurse called the extra bandage superficial and removed it as unnecessary.
reasons: Which knee was hurt says nothing about how deep the injury went.
A minor injury that affects only the outer skin needs just basic care.
An injury that reaches deep tissue and needs surgery is anything but shallow.
Something unnecessary is superfluous; the two words are easy to mix up.
